body:
Formation of extrusive landforms

Extrusive volcanic landforms develop when lava and fragmented volcanic materials reach the surface and accumulate. Their shapes depend principally on the viscosity of lava, the nature of eruptions, the arrangement of vents and the subsequent action of erosion.

Shield volcanoes

A shield volcano is a broad volcanic mountain with relatively gentle slopes. It forms through repeated outpourings of comparatively fluid lava, usually basaltic lava, which can spread over considerable distances.

Successive flows build a wide, low-gradient volcanic structure resembling a shield. Shield volcanoes can attain enormous volumes despite their comparatively gentle slopes.

Examples: Mauna Loa and Kilauea in Hawaii.

Composite volcanoes or stratovolcanoes

A composite volcano is a generally steep-sided volcanic mountain built by successive deposits of lava and fragmented volcanic material, including ash and other pyroclastic deposits.

Composite volcanoes are especially common in volcanic arcs associated with subduction zones. Their magma may be relatively viscous and gas-bearing, and their eruptions can be highly explosive.

Examples: Mount Fuji in Japan and Mount St. Helens in the United States.

Cinder cones

A cinder cone is a typically small, steep-sided volcanic cone formed mainly by the accumulation of loose volcanic fragments around a vent. The cone usually contains a summit crater.

Example: Paricutin in Mexico, which began forming in 1943.

Lava domes

A lava dome develops when highly viscous lava accumulates close to its vent because it cannot flow far. The resulting landform is steep and dome-shaped. Parts of a growing lava dome may collapse and generate dangerous pyroclastic currents.

Craters and calderas

A crater is a depression associated with a volcanic vent. It may be produced by explosive activity, excavation or collapse near the vent.

A caldera is a much larger volcanic depression, commonly formed when the ground above a magma storage region collapses following the withdrawal or eruption of substantial quantities of magma.

Calderas may contain lakes, smaller volcanic cones or renewed volcanic activity. They are not necessarily permanently extinct volcanic structures.

Example: Crater Lake in Oregon, United States, occupies a caldera formed by the collapse of an earlier volcano. Despite its name, its basin is a caldera rather than an ordinary small summit crater.

Lava plateaus and flood basalt provinces

Large fissure eruptions can discharge enormous quantities of fluid basaltic lava. The lava spreads over extensive areas and solidifies into broad sheets. Repeated episodes produce superimposed layers of basalt.

These accumulations create extensive volcanic plateaus called flood basalt provinces. Differential weathering and erosion of successive lava layers may produce characteristic step-like slopes.

The Deccan Traps of western and central India are a major example. Their main volcanic activity occurred around 66 million years ago, near the boundary between the Cretaceous and Paleogene geological periods.

Submarine volcanic landforms

Volcanic activity along mid-ocean ridges creates new oceanic crust. When basaltic lava erupts underwater and cools rapidly, it may form rounded masses known as pillow lavas.

Repeated submarine eruptions can also build volcanic mountains known as seamounts. Where such mountains rise above sea level, they may form volcanic islands.

Prelims focus

  • Shield volcanoes are broad and generally have gentle slopes.
  • Composite volcanoes contain layers of lava and fragmented volcanic deposits.
  • Paricutin is a Mexican cinder cone.
  • Calderas commonly form through collapse following magma withdrawal.
  • The Deccan Traps are an extensive flood basalt province.
  • Trap: The Deccan Traps were not formed by the growth of a single composite volcanic cone.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2026–27 reprint, Chapter 3, pp. 23–24; US Geological Survey, Principal Types of Volcanoes and Volcanoes of the United States; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Deccan Traps at Panchgani and Mahabaleshwar, Tentative List entry. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

body:
Formation of intrusive igneous bodies

Not all magma reaches the Earth's surface. Magma may enter fractures, occupy underground spaces or accumulate between existing rock layers. When it cools and solidifies underground, it forms intrusive igneous bodies.

These bodies may subsequently become visible at the surface when uplift, weathering and erosion remove the overlying rocks.

Concordant and discordant intrusions

The relationship between an intrusion and the surrounding rock layers is important in identifying its type.

  • Concordant intrusion: Broadly follows the arrangement of the existing rock layers.
  • Discordant intrusion: Cuts across existing rock layers or structures.

Batholiths

A batholith is an extremely large, irregular mass of intrusive igneous rock formed at considerable depth within the crust. Batholiths are commonly granitic in composition.

They may form the deeply rooted parts of mountain regions. Long periods of erosion can expose them at the surface.

Laccoliths

A laccolith forms when magma is injected between rock layers and accumulates sufficiently to bend the overlying layers upwards.

The resulting intrusive body is characteristically dome-shaped, with a relatively flat base and a curved upper surface. It represents underground magma accumulation rather than lava building an external volcanic cone.

Lopoliths

A lopolith is a large, saucer-shaped intrusive body in which the central portion lies lower than the surrounding margins. Its overall shape is concave upwards.

It can therefore be distinguished from a typical laccolith, which produces upward doming of the overlying strata. The alternative spelling lapolith is used in some textbooks.

Phacoliths

A phacolith is a lens-shaped intrusive body occupying favourable positions within folded rock layers, particularly the crests of anticlines or troughs of synclines.

An anticline is an upward-arching fold, whereas a syncline is a downward-curving fold. Magma may accumulate along the curved layers of these structures.

Sills

A sill is a sheet-like intrusion formed when magma enters between existing rock layers and solidifies approximately parallel to them.

Sills are frequently horizontal where the original rock layers are horizontal. However, a sill may be inclined if the surrounding strata are inclined. Its defining feature is its broadly concordant relationship with the host rock layers.

Dykes

A dyke is a sheet-like intrusion formed when magma enters a fracture that cuts across existing rocks and subsequently solidifies.

Dykes are frequently steep or nearly vertical, but their defining characteristic is their discordant relationship with the surrounding rock structures rather than an absolutely vertical orientation.

Dykes can act as pathways feeding surface lava eruptions. Extensive dyke systems are associated with the Deccan volcanic province of western India.

Intrusive and extrusive processes in the same volcanic system

A volcanic system may contain a deep magma storage region, dykes that carry magma upwards, sills that spread between rock layers and surface lava flows. These are connected manifestations of magma movement at different depths.

For example, a dyke can supply magma to a fissure eruption, producing extensive basaltic lava flows at the surface while the dyke itself solidifies underground.

A lava dome is an extrusive accumulation of viscous lava at the surface. A laccolith is an intrusive body that bends overlying rock layers upwards. Both may have a dome-like shape, but they form in different environments.

Prelims focus

  • Batholith: very large, deep intrusive mass, commonly granitic.
  • Laccolith: dome-shaped intrusion with a relatively flat base.
  • Lopolith: saucer-shaped intrusive body.
  • Phacolith: intrusion associated with anticline crests or syncline troughs.
  • Sill follows rock layers; dyke cuts across them.
  • Trap: A sill need not be perfectly horizontal, and a dyke need not be perfectly vertical.

[References: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, 2018–19 reprint, Chapter 2, pp. 7–9; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2026–27 reprint, Chapter 3, Volcanic Landforms and Intrusive Forms, pp. 24–25; V. N. Kulkarni, Geology of Gujarat, Government of Gujarat, 1985, Geomorphology and Geological Formations. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

body:
Why volcanoes occur in particular regions

Volcanism is geographically concentrated because magma generation requires particular geological conditions. Many volcanoes occur along tectonic plate boundaries, while some develop within plates above volcanic hotspots.

Volcanoes at convergent boundaries

When an oceanic plate descends beneath another plate, water and other volatile substances released from the descending plate promote partial melting of the overlying mantle.

The resulting magma may rise through the overlying plate and produce a curved chain of volcanoes known as a volcanic arc.

  • Oceanic–continental convergence: May produce a continental volcanic arc. The Andes of western South America are an example.
  • Oceanic–oceanic convergence: May produce a volcanic island arc. The Aleutian island arc is an example; Japan's main island arcs involve subduction beneath continental crust.

Subduction-related volcanoes commonly include composite volcanoes capable of explosive eruptions. Deep ocean trenches frequently occur on the seaward side of volcanic arcs.

Volcanoes at divergent boundaries

Where tectonic plates move apart, hot mantle rises into the space beneath the separating plates. The reduction in pressure promotes partial melting and the formation of predominantly basaltic magma.

At mid-ocean ridges, this magma produces new oceanic crust. A considerable amount of volcanic activity therefore takes place beneath the oceans and is not visible above sea level.

Important examples include the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and volcanic regions of the East African Rift, where continental crust is undergoing extension.

Transform boundaries

At transform boundaries, plates move horizontally past one another. These boundaries commonly produce shallow earthquakes but do not ordinarily generate extensive volcanism through plate movement alone.

The San Andreas Fault in California is an important example of a transform boundary.

Hotspot volcanism

A hotspot is a region of persistent volcanic activity that can occur independently of the immediate boundaries between tectonic plates. Many hotspots are associated with unusually hot material rising within the mantle.

As a tectonic plate moves over a comparatively persistent source of magma, a sequence of volcanoes may develop. Older volcanoes are carried away from the principal region of magma supply while newer volcanoes form closer to it.

The Hawaiian volcanic island chain illustrates this process. Yellowstone in the United States is an example of continental hotspot-related volcanism. Iceland is unusual because its volcanism is associated with both a divergent mid-ocean ridge and a hotspot.

Principal volcanic regions

Pacific Ring of Fire

This is a major concentration of volcanoes around the margins of the Pacific Ocean. Important regions include the Andes, western North America, the Aleutian Islands, Japan, the Philippines, parts of Indonesia and New Zealand.

Much of the volcanic activity results from subduction of oceanic plates. The Ring of Fire is also a major earthquake belt.

Mediterranean volcanic region

The Mediterranean region contains important volcanoes associated with the complex convergence of tectonic plates. Mount Etna in Sicily and Mount Vesuvius near Naples, both in Italy, are well-known examples.

Atlantic and East African volcanic regions

Volcanic activity along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and in Iceland illustrates divergent-boundary volcanism. The East African Rift illustrates volcanism associated with continental extension.

Earthquake and volcano distribution compared

Earthquakes and volcanoes overlap geographically in many regions, particularly at subduction zones and divergent boundaries. However, their distributions are not identical.

Transform boundaries may experience frequent earthquakes without extensive volcanic activity. Similarly, the Himalayan continental collision zone is highly seismic but does not contain a continuous chain of active volcanoes comparable to the volcanic arcs around the Pacific.

Hotspot volcanism can produce volcanoes in the interiors of tectonic plates, just as existing intraplate faults can produce earthquakes away from plate boundaries.

Prelims focus

  • The Andes are associated with oceanic–continental subduction.
  • Japan and the Aleutian Islands illustrate volcanic island arcs.
  • Mid-ocean ridge volcanism is predominantly basaltic.
  • Hawaii is a classic example of oceanic hotspot volcanism.
  • Iceland combines divergent-boundary and hotspot activity.
  • Trap: All earthquake belts are not necessarily volcanic belts.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2026–27 reprint, Chapter 3, Mid-Ocean Ridge Volcanoes; NOAA JetStream, Plate Tectonics and Earthquakes; US Geological Survey, This Dynamic Earth: The Story of Plate Tectonics, Hotspots and Pacific Ring of Fire. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]
